# Lumexa Mission Log: Programming Foundations with C

**Course/Path:** Programming Foundations with C
**Lesson:** 08 of 08
**Title:** Structures, File Handling, Debugging and Project Development
**Duration:** 60 minutes
**Difficulty:** Intermediate
**Technology:** C (gcc)

---

## Mission Brief

Your SRMS keeps a student's name in one array, the marks in another and the total in a third. Rename a student, delete one, sort them, and you must keep three arrays in step: forget one and the data is silently wrong. Worse, when you close the program, **everything vanishes**. A result system that forgets its results is not a result system.

This final lesson of the course fixes both problems. A **structure** groups the pieces of one student into a single unit. **File handling** makes the data survive after the program ends. And because a finished program is more than the sum of its parts, you will also learn how professionals **find bugs systematically** and how a larger program is **planned, built and tested step by step**. At the end of the lesson you assemble everything from the past seven lessons into the complete **Student Result Management System**.

## Learning Objectives

1. Define a `struct` and a `typedef`, create arrays of structures and access members with `.` and `->`.
2. Open, write, read and close text files with `fopen`, `fprintf`, `fscanf`, `fgets` and `fclose`, checking for errors.
3. Design a simple file format and save and load a list of records.
4. Apply a systematic debugging method using print statements, compiler warnings, assertions and a debugger.
5. Plan a program from requirements to a function design, and build and test it in small increments.
6. Assemble the complete menu-driven SRMS from the pieces built in this course.

## Prerequisites

- Lesson 7: pointers, `malloc`/`realloc`/`free` and pointer parameters (structures are usually passed by pointer).
- Lessons 1 to 6: the grade functions, loops, menus, strings and arrays you will now combine.

## Concept Explanation

### Structures: one name for related data

A **structure** (`struct`) groups variables of different types under one name. Each variable inside is a **member**:

```c
struct Student {
    int roll;
    char name[30];
    int marks[3];
    int total;
};

struct Student a = {101, "Anika Rahman", {72, 65, 90}, 0};
printf("%s has roll %d\n", a.name, a.roll);   // the dot reaches a member
```

A structure is a **new type** that you design. A `typedef` gives it a shorter name, so you can write `Student` instead of `struct Student`:

```c
typedef struct {
    int roll;
    char name[30];
    int marks[3];
    int total;
} Student;
```

You can make arrays of structures (`Student class_list[40]`), allocate them on the heap (`malloc(n * sizeof(Student))`), and assign one structure to another with `=` (the whole thing is copied, including the arrays inside it).

### Structures and pointers

Passing a big structure by value copies all of it. It is cheaper, and necessary if the function must change it, to pass a **pointer**. To reach a member through a pointer, use the **arrow operator** `->`:

```c
void evaluate(Student *s)
{
    s->total = s->marks[0] + s->marks[1] + s->marks[2];   // same as (*s).total
}
/* call: evaluate(&a); */
```

`s->total` means "the `total` member of the structure that `s` points to". Use `const Student *s` when a function only needs to read.

### Files: data that survives

A **file** stores data on disk. In C you work with a **file pointer** of type `FILE *`:

| Step | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Open | `FILE *f = fopen("data.txt", "w");` | `"r"` read, `"w"` write (erases the file), `"a"` append |
| Check | `if (f == NULL) { ... }` | the file may be missing or locked: always test |
| Use | `fprintf(f, ...)`, `fscanf(f, ...)`, `fgets(line, size, f)` | like `printf`, `scanf` and `fgets`, with the file as the first or last argument |
| Close | `fclose(f);` | flushes the data to disk and releases the file |

A text file is human-readable, so you can open it in an editor and see exactly what your program saved. Forgetting `fclose` can lose the last data; forgetting the `NULL` check crashes the program when a file is missing.

### Designing a file format

A program must be able to read back what it wrote, so decide on a **format**. A simple, popular choice is one record per line with a separator that cannot appear in the data, such as `|`:

```text
101|Anika Rahman|72|65|90
102|Rafi Ahmed|85|28|60
```

To read a line back, `sscanf(line, "%d|%29[^|]|%d|%d|%d", ...)` splits it. The pattern `%29[^|]` means "read up to 29 characters that are not a `|`", which allows names with spaces. Only save the **inputs** (roll, name, marks); recalculate the totals and GPA when loading, so the file can never disagree with the grade rules.

### Debugging: a method, not luck

A **bug** is a difference between what you meant and what the program does. Finding it by randomly changing code wastes hours. Use a method:

1. **Reproduce** it with the smallest input that fails, every time.
2. **Read the evidence**: the compiler message, the line number, the exact wrong output.
3. **Form a hypothesis** ("I think the loop skips the last mark") and **test** it, usually by printing the variables: `printf("i=%d sum=%d\n", i, sum);`. This is **print debugging**.
4. **Fix one thing**, then re-run the failing case *and* the earlier tests (a **regression test**).

Powerful helpers: compile with `gcc -Wall -Wextra -g` and read every warning; use `assert(index >= 0 && index < n);` from `<assert.h>` to stop the program at a broken assumption; compile with `-fsanitize=address,undefined` to catch memory and arithmetic errors; and learn a **debugger**. With `gdb` you can `break main`, `run`, `next` (one line), `print sum`, and `backtrace` to see how you got here. Explaining the code aloud to someone (or a rubber duck) is surprisingly effective.

### Project development: from requirements to a working system

Large programs are built in an order that keeps them working:

1. **Requirements**: what must the system do? (Add, list, search, topper, statistics, save, load.)
2. **Design**: choose the data (`Student`, `Roster`) and a function for each job, with its parameters and results, before writing any bodies.
3. **Build incrementally**: write one function, test it alone, and only then add the next. After each step the program should still compile and run.
4. **Test** with normal data, boundary data and bad data (empty class, invalid roll, missing file).
5. **Polish and document**: clear names, comments that say *why*, and a short note on how to use it.

Professional teams add **version control** (such as Git, which you will meet in Course 7) so that every working step is saved and can be restored.

## Key Vocabulary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Structure (`struct`)** | A user-defined type that groups variables, called members, under one name. |
| **Member** | One variable inside a structure. |
| **`typedef`** | A declaration that gives an existing type a new name. |
| **Arrow operator (`->`)** | Reaches a member through a pointer to a structure. |
| **File pointer (`FILE *`)** | A handle that represents an open file. |
| **Text file** | A file whose bytes are readable characters. |
| **File format** | The agreed layout of the data inside a file. |
| **Debugging** | Finding and fixing the cause of a bug. |
| **Regression test** | Re-running earlier tests after a change to prove nothing else broke. |
| **Assertion** | A check that stops the program if an assumption is false. |
| **Requirement** | A statement of something the system must do. |
| **Incremental development** | Building a program in small, tested steps. |

## Worked Examples

### Example 1: Structures and the arrow operator

```c
#include <stdio.h>

#define SUBJECTS 3

typedef struct {
    int roll;
    char name[30];
    int marks[SUBJECTS];
} Student;

int total_of(const Student *s)
{
    int t = 0;
    for (int j = 0; j < SUBJECTS; j++) {
        t += s->marks[j];
    }
    return t;
}

int main(void)
{
    Student a = {101, "Anika Rahman", {72, 65, 90}};
    Student list[2] = {a, {102, "Rafi Ahmed", {85, 28, 60}}};

    printf("%d %s %d\n", a.roll, a.name, total_of(&a));
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
        printf("%d: %s -> %d\n", list[i].roll, list[i].name, total_of(&list[i]));
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```output
101 Anika Rahman 227
101: Anika Rahman -> 227
102: Rafi Ahmed -> 173
```

1. `Student` is one type holding an int, a string and an array of marks. A **variable** `a` of this type holds them all together.
2. `a.roll` reaches a member of a variable; `s->marks[j]` reaches a member through a pointer. The two forms mean the same.
3. `list` is an array of two students; the first element is a *copy* of `a`. `list[i].name` is the name of student `i`.
4. `total_of` takes a pointer so the whole structure is not copied, and `const` promises it will not change it.

### Example 2: A file round trip

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    FILE *out = fopen("demo.txt", "w");
    if (out == NULL) {
        printf("Cannot open the file.\n");
        return 1;
    }
    fprintf(out, "Anika 72 65 90\n");
    fprintf(out, "Rafi 85 28 60\n");
    fclose(out);

    FILE *in = fopen("demo.txt", "r");
    if (in == NULL) {
        printf("Cannot read the file.\n");
        return 1;
    }
    char name[30];
    int a, b, c;
    while (fscanf(in, "%29s %d %d %d", name, &a, &b, &c) == 4) {
        printf("%s: total %d\n", name, a + b + c);
    }
    fclose(in);
    return 0;
}
```

```output
Anika: total 227
Rafi: total 173
```

1. Opening with `"w"` creates the file (or erases an existing one). Both `fopen` calls are checked for `NULL`.
2. `fprintf` works exactly like `printf`, with the file as its first argument.
3. `fscanf` returns the **number of items it read**. The loop continues while it reads 4 values and stops at the end of the file, because it then returns less than 4.
4. Both files are closed. Run the program and open `demo.txt` in an editor to see the data your program wrote.

### Example 3: Debugging a program that gives a wrong answer

This program should print the total and the average of five marks. It compiles without a warning, but the answer is wrong.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int marks[5] = {72, 65, 90, 41, 58};
    int n = 5;
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
        sum += marks[i];
    }
    double average = sum / n;
    printf("Total: %d\nAverage: %.2f\n", sum, average);
    return 0;
}
```

```output
Total: 268
Average: 53.00
```

1. **Reproduce and read the evidence.** The correct total is 72 + 65 + 90 + 41 + 58 = 326 and the average is 65.20. The program prints 268 and 53.00: both are wrong.
2. **Hypothesis 1:** a mark is being skipped. 326 − 268 = 58, which is the last mark. Test it by printing inside the loop: `printf("i=%d sum=%d\n", i, sum);` shows `i` going from 0 to 3 only, so the loop ends one pass early. The condition should be `i < n`.
3. **Hypothesis 2:** even with the right total, 326 / 5 would give 65, not 65.20, because both operands are integers (Lesson 2). The fix is a cast.
4. **Fix both, then re-run.** One change at a time, with the failing case checked after each.

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void)
{
    int marks[5] = {72, 65, 90, 41, 58};
    int n = 5;
    int sum = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        sum += marks[i];
    }
    double average = (double)sum / n;
    printf("Total: %d\nAverage: %.2f\n", sum, average);
    return 0;
}
```

```output
Total: 326
Average: 65.20
```

## Common Mistakes and Misconceptions

- **Using `.` on a pointer, or `->` on a variable.** `s.total` where `s` is a `Student *` fails to compile. Use `->` for pointers and `.` for variables.
- **Forgetting `fclose`.** Data may stay in a buffer and never reach the disk, and you may run out of open files. Close every file you open.
- **Not checking `fopen`.** A missing file returns `NULL`; using it crashes. Always test and print a clear message.
- **Opening with `"w"` by accident.** `"w"` erases the file immediately. To add records, use `"a"`; to read, `"r"`.
- **Saving calculated values.** If you save the GPA and later change the grade rules, the file disagrees with the code. Save the inputs and recalculate.
- **A separator that can appear in the data.** If names could contain `|`, the format breaks. Choose a separator that cannot occur, or forbid it on input.
- **Changing many things at once while debugging.** You will not know which change helped. Change one thing, then test.
- **Assuming "it compiles" means "it works".** The compiler checks grammar, not meaning. Test with known answers and boundary data.
- **Writing the whole program before testing anything.** Build and test one function at a time.

## Guided Hands-On Activity

**Structures, files and a bug hunt.** Work with your teacher.

1. Type Example 1. Add a `double average` member to `Student`, write `void evaluate(Student *s)` that fills `total` and `average` through the pointer, and call it for both students.
2. Type Example 2 and run it. Open `demo.txt` in a text editor and check that its contents match what you expected. Then change the first `fopen` mode to `"a"`, run twice, and explain what happened to the file.
3. Make the program fail on purpose: change the file name in the second `fopen` to a file that does not exist. Does your `NULL` check catch it? What would have happened without the check?
4. Type the **buggy** version of Example 3 and *do not read the explanation*. Find the two bugs yourself with print statements, and write down each hypothesis and the test that confirmed it.
5. Add `#include <assert.h>` and, inside the loop, `assert(i >= 0 && i < 5);`. Then change the loop condition to `i <= n` and run: what does the assertion say?
6. Compile the program with `-fsanitize=address,undefined -g` while the loop reads `i <= n`. Read the report and name the exact kind of error.
7. If your teacher provides `gdb`, start it with `gdb ./a.out`, type `break main`, `run`, then `next` a few times and `print sum` to watch the variable change.

## Lesson Project: SRMS: The Complete System

### Objective

Assemble the finished **Student Result Management System**: a menu-driven C program that stores students as structures in a growing heap array, applies the Bangladesh grade rules, answers questions about the class, and saves to and loads from a file. It uses every idea of the course: variables, decisions, loops, functions, arrays and strings, pointers and dynamic memory, structures and files.

### Requirements

- Use `typedef struct` for `Student` (roll number, name, three marks, total, GPA and a passed flag) and a `Roster` structure that holds a pointer to a heap array, a `count` and a `capacity`.
- Grow the array with `realloc` (start with room for 2 and double when full), check every allocation, and `free` the array before the program ends.
- The menu has these options: `1 Add`, `2 List`, `3 Find`, `4 Topper`, `5 Stats`, `6 Save`, `7 Load` and `0 Exit`, handled with a `switch`, and an invalid choice prints `Please choose a number from 0 to 7.`
- **Add** reads a roll number (positive, not already used), a name with spaces and three marks, validates them (0 to 100) and rejects bad data with a clear message.
- Use the grade rules from Lessons 3 and 5: a student passes only if every mark is at least 33; the GPA is the average of the grade points, or 0.00 for a fail.
- **Save** writes one line per student as `roll|name|m1|m2|m3`; **Load** reads them back and recalculates totals and GPA. Both must report errors if the file cannot be opened.
- Every function has one job and a prototype or a definition above its first use; no function is longer than about 30 lines.

### Instructions

1. **Plan.** On paper, list your functions with their parameters and results: `read_line`, `grade_point`, `evaluate`, `roster_add`, `find_by_roll`, `add_student`, `list_all`, `search_student`, `show_topper`, `show_stats`, `save_roster`, `load_roster`, and `main`.
2. **Step 1.** Write the structures and `evaluate`, and test it with one hard-coded student printed from `main`.
3. **Step 2.** Add `roster_add` with `realloc`, `list_all` and `print_student`. Test by adding three hard-coded students.
4. **Step 3.** Write `add_student` with validation, and the menu loop with `Add`, `List` and `Exit`.
5. **Step 4.** Add `find_by_roll` (returning a pointer or `NULL`), then `Find`, `Topper` and `Stats`.
6. **Step 5.** Write `save_roster` and `load_roster`, using `fprintf` and `fgets` with `sscanf`.
7. **Step 6.** Test with normal data, an empty class, a duplicate roll, an invalid mark and a missing file. Compile with `-Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address,undefined -g` and fix every report.
8. **Step 7.** Write a five-line `README` comment at the top of the file: what the program does, how to compile it and the input format.

### Expected Output

For this session of menu choices and data (`1`, roll `101`, `Anika Rahman`, `72 65 90`; `1`, roll `102`, `Rafi Ahmed`, `85 28 60`; then `2`, `3` with `102`, `4`, `5`, `6`, `7`, `2`, an invalid `9`, and `0`) the program prints:

### Hints

1. **Hint 1 (a crash when adding the third student).** Check `roster_add`: when `count == capacity` you must call `realloc` and store the new pointer. A pointer to an old element (for example one returned by `find_by_roll`) becomes invalid after the array moves.
2. **Hint 2 (the name reads as empty).** A `scanf` left a newline in the input. Read every line with `read_line` and extract numbers with `sscanf`, as in Lesson 6.
3. **Hint 3 (load gives garbage).** Check the `sscanf` pattern: `"%d|%29[^|]|%d|%d|%d"` and that you compare its result with 5. Zero the structure first with `memset(&s, 0, sizeof s);`.
4. **Hint 4 (the GPA differs after loading).** Call `evaluate(&s)` after reading, so the totals and GPA are recalculated from the marks.
5. **Hint 5 (the sanitiser reports a leak).** The array in `Roster` must be freed once, at the end of `main`. A `return` in the middle of `main` must free it too.
6. **Hint 6 (`Find` prints the wrong student).** `find_by_roll` compares the *roll number*, not the position. Print `s->roll` to check.

### Success Criteria

- [ ] All eight menu options work, and an invalid choice gets the right message.
- [ ] Students are stored in a heap array that grows by doubling, and nothing is leaked (a sanitiser run is silent).
- [ ] Marks outside 0 to 100, a duplicate or invalid roll and a missing file are all handled with a clear message and no crash.
- [ ] After Save and Load the list shows exactly the same students, totals, GPAs and results.
- [ ] The grade rules are the Bangladesh rules from Lesson 3: the pass mark is 33 in every subject and a failed student has a GPA of 0.00.
- [ ] Every function has one job, and I tested each one before adding the next.
- [ ] The code compiles with `-Wall -Wextra` with no warnings, and the top of the file explains how to use it.

### Extension Challenge

Add three professional features: **(a)** option `8 Delete a student` that removes a roll number by shifting the later elements down; **(b)** option `9 Sort` that lists students by total, highest first, using a nested loop to swap structures (copy the whole `Student` with `=`); **(c)** a **binary file** format using `fwrite` and `fread` for the whole `Student` array, and a short note comparing it with your text format: which is easier to inspect, and which is faster? Then measure the file sizes for 1,000 students.

## Lesson Recap

- A **structure** groups related data of different types into one new type; use `.` on a variable and `->` on a pointer, and pass big structures by pointer.
- **Files** make data survive: `fopen` (check for `NULL`), `fprintf`/`fscanf`/`fgets`, `fclose`; save the *inputs* in a clear format and recalculate the rest.
- Debug with a **method**: reproduce, read the evidence, form a hypothesis, test it, fix one thing, re-run all tests; use warnings, assertions, sanitisers and a debugger.
- Build large programs **incrementally**: requirements, design, one tested function at a time, then polish and document.
- You can now build a complete C application using variables, decisions, loops, functions, arrays, strings, pointers, dynamic memory, structures and files.

## Homework / Extension Mission

Finish the complete SRMS and give it a final test pass using a written **test plan**: a table of at least twelve cases (a normal student, a failing student, a student with a mark of exactly 33 and 32, an invalid mark, a duplicate roll, an empty class, a missing file, a class of 100 students, and so on) with the expected result of each and a tick when it passes. Then write a one-page **user guide** that explains each menu option. Finally, prepare a three-minute demonstration of your SRMS for the first lesson of the next course, where you will also name the three parts of the program you are proudest of and the one you would redesign.

## Course Project Connection

This lesson **is** the course project: the finished **Student Result Management System using C**. Everything you built across the eight lessons is inside it. The algorithm and flowchart from Lesson 1 became the `evaluate` logic; input and arithmetic from Lesson 2 became `add_student`; the grade ladder from Lesson 3 and the functions from Lesson 5 became `grade_point` and the passed rule; the menu and loops from Lesson 4 became `main`; arrays and strings from Lesson 6 became names and marks; pointers and `realloc` from Lesson 7 became the growing roster; and structures and files from today completed the system. Keep it: you will be asked to present it, and in Course 2 you will rebuild a similar system with classes.

## Instructor-Guided Teaching Notes

**Pacing (60 minutes).** 10 minutes: structures and `->`. 10 minutes: files and the format. 10 minutes: the debugging method and Example 3. 30 minutes: the project, as a guided build in steps; this lesson is the capstone and most of the work continues at home.

**Live demonstrations.** Open `srms_data.txt` in a text editor after saving to show the data. Debug Example 3 live, asking students for hypotheses. Show gdb's `break`, `next` and `print` on the buggy program.

**Misconceptions.** "A structure variable is a pointer." "A file is loaded by `fopen`" (it only opens a handle). "The compiler finds logic errors."

**Assessment of the project.** Mark against the Success Criteria; ask each student to explain one function aloud and to demonstrate a failing input. Look for single-purpose functions, `NULL` checks and a silent sanitiser run.

**Reference solution `srms.c`** (compile with `gcc -std=c11 -Wall -Wextra srms.c -o srms`; it writes `srms_data.txt` in the current folder):

```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

#define SUBJECTS 3
#define NAME_LEN 30
#define PASS_MARK 33
#define DATA_FILE "srms_data.txt"

typedef struct {
    int roll;
    char name[NAME_LEN];
    int marks[SUBJECTS];
    int total;
    double gpa;
    int passed;
} Student;

typedef struct {
    Student *items;
    int count;
    int capacity;
} Roster;

static void read_line(char *buf, int size)
{
    if (fgets(buf, size, stdin) == NULL) {
        buf[0] = '\0';
        return;
    }
    buf[strcspn(buf, "\n")] = '\0';
}

static double grade_point(int mark)
{
    if (mark >= 80) return 5.0;
    if (mark >= 70) return 4.0;
    if (mark >= 60) return 3.5;
    if (mark >= 50) return 3.0;
    if (mark >= 40) return 2.0;
    if (mark >= PASS_MARK) return 1.0;
    return 0.0;
}

static void evaluate(Student *s)
{
    double points = 0.0;
    s->total = 0;
    s->passed = 1;
    for (int j = 0; j < SUBJECTS; j++) {
        s->total += s->marks[j];
        points += grade_point(s->marks[j]);
        if (s->marks[j] < PASS_MARK) {
            s->passed = 0;
        }
    }
    s->gpa = s->passed ? points / SUBJECTS : 0.0;
}

static int roster_add(Roster *r, Student s)
{
    if (r->count == r->capacity) {
        int bigger = r->capacity == 0 ? 2 : r->capacity * 2;
        Student *items = realloc(r->items, (size_t)bigger * sizeof *items);
        if (items == NULL) {
            return 0;
        }
        r->items = items;
        r->capacity = bigger;
    }
    r->items[r->count++] = s;
    return 1;
}

static Student *find_by_roll(Roster *r, int roll)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < r->count; i++) {
        if (r->items[i].roll == roll) {
            return &r->items[i];
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

static void print_header(void)
{
    printf("%-5s %-14s %6s %7s %4s %5s %5s %s\n", "Roll", "Name", "Bangla", "English", "Math", "Total", "GPA", "Result");
}

static void print_student(const Student *s)
{
    printf("%-5d %-14s %6d %7d %4d %5d %5.2f %s\n", s->roll, s->name, s->marks[0], s->marks[1], s->marks[2], s->total,
           s->gpa, s->passed ? "PASS" : "FAIL");
}

static void add_student(Roster *r)
{
    Student s;
    char line[100];
    memset(&s, 0, sizeof s);
    printf("Roll number:\n");
    read_line(line, sizeof line);
    if (sscanf(line, "%d", &s.roll) != 1 || s.roll < 1) {
        printf("Invalid roll number.\n");
        return;
    }
    if (find_by_roll(r, s.roll) != NULL) {
        printf("Roll %d already exists.\n", s.roll);
        return;
    }
    printf("Name:\n");
    read_line(s.name, NAME_LEN);
    printf("Marks (Bangla English Math):\n");
    read_line(line, sizeof line);
    if (sscanf(line, "%d %d %d", &s.marks[0], &s.marks[1], &s.marks[2]) != SUBJECTS) {
        printf("Please enter three numbers.\n");
        return;
    }
    for (int j = 0; j < SUBJECTS; j++) {
        if (s.marks[j] < 0 || s.marks[j] > 100) {
            printf("Invalid mark: marks must be between 0 and 100.\n");
            return;
        }
    }
    evaluate(&s);
    if (roster_add(r, s)) {
        printf("Added %s.\n", s.name);
    } else {
        printf("Out of memory.\n");
    }
}

static void list_all(const Roster *r)
{
    if (r->count == 0) {
        printf("No students yet.\n");
        return;
    }
    print_header();
    for (int i = 0; i < r->count; i++) {
        print_student(&r->items[i]);
    }
}

static void search_student(Roster *r)
{
    char line[100];
    int roll;
    printf("Roll number to find:\n");
    read_line(line, sizeof line);
    if (sscanf(line, "%d", &roll) != 1) {
        printf("Invalid roll number.\n");
        return;
    }
    Student *s = find_by_roll(r, roll);
    if (s == NULL) {
        printf("No student with roll %d.\n", roll);
        return;
    }
    print_header();
    print_student(s);
}

static void show_topper(const Roster *r)
{
    if (r->count == 0) {
        printf("No students yet.\n");
        return;
    }
    int best = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < r->count; i++) {
        if (r->items[i].total > r->items[best].total) {
            best = i;
        }
    }
    printf("Topper: %s (roll %d) with %d marks.\n", r->items[best].name, r->items[best].roll, r->items[best].total);
}

static void show_stats(const Roster *r)
{
    if (r->count == 0) {
        printf("No students yet.\n");
        return;
    }
    long sum = 0;
    int passed = 0;
    int high = r->items[0].total, low = r->items[0].total;
    for (int i = 0; i < r->count; i++) {
        sum += r->items[i].total;
        passed += r->items[i].passed;
        if (r->items[i].total > high) high = r->items[i].total;
        if (r->items[i].total < low) low = r->items[i].total;
    }
    printf("Students: %d, passed: %d, failed: %d\n", r->count, passed, r->count - passed);
    printf("Average total: %.2f, highest: %d, lowest: %d\n", (double)sum / r->count, high, low);
}

static int save_roster(const Roster *r, const char *path)
{
    FILE *f = fopen(path, "w");
    if (f == NULL) {
        return 0;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < r->count; i++) {
        const Student *s = &r->items[i];
        fprintf(f, "%d|%s|%d|%d|%d\n", s->roll, s->name, s->marks[0], s->marks[1], s->marks[2]);
    }
    fclose(f);
    return 1;
}

static int load_roster(Roster *r, const char *path)
{
    FILE *f = fopen(path, "r");
    char line[200];
    if (f == NULL) {
        return -1;
    }
    r->count = 0;
    while (fgets(line, sizeof line, f) != NULL) {
        Student s;
        memset(&s, 0, sizeof s);
        line[strcspn(line, "\n")] = '\0';
        if (sscanf(line, "%d|%29[^|]|%d|%d|%d", &s.roll, s.name, &s.marks[0], &s.marks[1], &s.marks[2]) == 5) {
            evaluate(&s);
            roster_add(r, s);
        }
    }
    fclose(f);
    return r->count;
}

int main(void)
{
    Roster roster = {NULL, 0, 0};
    char line[100];
    int choice;

    do {
        printf("\nSRMS menu: 1 Add | 2 List | 3 Find | 4 Topper | 5 Stats | 6 Save | 7 Load | 0 Exit\nChoice:\n");
        read_line(line, sizeof line);
        if (sscanf(line, "%d", &choice) != 1) {
            choice = -1;
        }
        switch (choice) {
            case 1: add_student(&roster); break;
            case 2: list_all(&roster); break;
            case 3: search_student(&roster); break;
            case 4: show_topper(&roster); break;
            case 5: show_stats(&roster); break;
            case 6:
                if (save_roster(&roster, DATA_FILE)) {
                    printf("Saved %d student(s) to %s.\n", roster.count, DATA_FILE);
                } else {
                    printf("Could not write %s.\n", DATA_FILE);
                }
                break;
            case 7: {
                int n = load_roster(&roster, DATA_FILE);
                if (n < 0) {
                    printf("Could not open %s.\n", DATA_FILE);
                } else {
                    printf("Loaded %d student(s) from %s.\n", n, DATA_FILE);
                }
                break;
            }
            case 0: printf("Goodbye!\n"); break;
            default: printf("Please choose a number from 0 to 7.\n");
        }
    } while (choice != 0);

    free(roster.items);
    return 0;
}
```

# Lumexa Mission Log: Object-Oriented Programming & Programming Languages

**Course/Path:** Object-Oriented Programming & Programming Languages
**Lesson:** 01 of 08
**Title:** Introduction to C++ and Procedural vs Object-Oriented Programming
**Duration:** 60 minutes
**Difficulty:** Beginner to Intermediate
**Technology:** C++ (g++)

---

## Mission Brief

A school library wants a small system to keep track of its books: who has borrowed what, and how many copies are left. You already know how to do this in C: a `struct`, an array and a handful of functions. In this course you will build that system twice, first the way you already know and then the way professional teams build large programs: with **objects**.

Today you start with the familiar way, now written in **C++**. It will work, and that is the point. As you build it, notice how the data and the functions that use it drift apart, and how easily one careless line can put the library into an impossible state, such as a book with minus five copies. That pain is exactly the problem that **object-oriented programming** was invented to solve.

## Learning Objectives

1. Explain how C++ relates to C, and compile and run a C++ program with `g++`.
2. Use `cin`, `cout`, `getline`, `std::string` and `std::vector` for input, output and collections.
3. Pass arguments by value, by reference and by `const` reference, and choose between them.
4. Describe procedural programming and name three weaknesses that appear as a program grows.
5. Describe the object-oriented idea (objects, classes and the four pillars) and compare it with procedural design.
6. Build the procedural version of the library catalogue as the baseline for the course project.

## Prerequisites

- Course 1: functions, arrays, structures and the habit of testing a program with known data.
- The `g++` compiler (or the C++ Code Lab, when your teacher has it enabled).

## Concept Explanation

### From C to C++

C++ was created by Bjarne Stroustrup in the early 1980s as "C with Classes". It keeps C's speed and most of its syntax, and adds tools for building large programs: **classes** and objects, a **standard library** (strings, vectors, algorithms), **references**, **templates** and **exceptions**. C++ source files end in `.cpp`, and you compile them with `g++`:

```text
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra main.cpp -o main
```

Most of the C you wrote in Course 1 still compiles as C++, but good C++ replaces risky C tools with safer ones:

| Task | In C (Course 1) | In C++ |
|---|---|---|
| Output | `printf("%d\n", n);` | `cout << n << '\n';` |
| Input | `scanf("%d", &n);` | `cin >> n;` |
| Text | `char name[30];` | `string name;` |
| Growing list | `malloc` and `realloc` | `vector<int> v; v.push_back(5);` |
| Memory clean-up | you call `free` | the library does it for you |

### Input and output with iostream

The header `<iostream>` provides `cout` (output) and `cin` (input). The operator `<<` sends values to `cout`, and `>>` takes them from `cin`. The standard library lives in the **namespace** `std`; writing `using namespace std;` at the top lets you leave out the `std::` prefix.

```cpp
int copies;
cout << "Copies: ";
cin >> copies;
cout << "You entered " << copies << '\n';
```

`cin >> x` stops at whitespace, so it reads one word. To read a whole line, including spaces, use `getline(cin, line);`. If you read a number with `>>` and then call `getline`, the newline left behind is read as an empty line: call `cin.ignore();` in between. To align columns, include `<iomanip>` and use `setw(10)` and `left`.

### Strings and vectors

`std::string` holds text of any length. You join strings with `+`, compare them with `==`, and ask for `title.size()`. `std::vector<T>` is a list that grows by itself:

```cpp
vector<string> titles = {"Python Basics", "Digital Logic"};
titles.push_back("World Atlas");      // add at the end
cout << titles.size() << '\n';        // 3
for (const string& t : titles) {      // visit every element
    cout << t << '\n';
}
```

The loop `for (const string& t : titles)` is a **range-based for**: it visits every element without an index. `auto` lets the compiler work out a type for you (`auto n = titles.size();`).

### References and function parameters

By default C++ passes a **copy** of each argument, just like C. A **reference** parameter (`int& x`) is another name for the caller's variable, so the function can change it without the pointer syntax you met in Course 1. A **`const` reference** (`const vector<string>& v`) avoids the copy of a large object and promises not to change it.

| Parameter | Copies the argument? | Can change the caller's value? | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `int x` | yes | no | small values such as numbers |
| `int& x` | no | yes | a result the function must change |
| `const string& s` | no | no | big objects that are only read |

### Procedural programming, and where it hurts

In **procedural programming** you organise a program as a list of steps: data lives in variables and structures, and functions act on it. That is how you built the SRMS, and it works very well for small programs. As a program grows, three problems appear:

1. **No protection.** Any function (or any line in `main`) can change any value, even to something that makes no sense.
2. **Data and behaviour are separate.** Nothing links a `Book` to the functions that are allowed to change it; you must remember to pass the right data to the right function.
3. **Copy and paste to extend.** A new kind of item, such as a magazine, needs its own functions or long `if` chains, and a change to a book has to be repeated everywhere.

### Object-oriented programming: the big idea

In **object-oriented programming (OOP)** you design around *things*. An **object** bundles some data with the functions that work on that data; a **class** is the blueprint from which objects are made. The data can be hidden behind a small, safe interface, so that other code can only change it in ways the object allows. OOP rests on four ideas that you will meet one by one in this course: **encapsulation**, **abstraction**, **inheritance** and **polymorphism**.

| | Procedural | Object-oriented |
|---|---|---|
| Main question | "What steps must happen?" | "What things exist, and what can each do?" |
| Unit of design | the function | the object (data + functions) |
| Who may change the data? | any function | only the object's own functions |
| Adding a new kind of item | copy and edit functions | create a new class |

## Key Vocabulary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **C++** | A compiled language that extends C with classes, a standard library and safer tools. |
| **Namespace** | A named group of names; the standard library lives in `std`. |
| **`std::string`** | A library type that stores text of any length. |
| **`std::vector`** | A library type for a list that grows automatically. |
| **Reference (`&`)** | A second name for an existing variable. |
| **`const` reference** | A reference that reads the original without copying or changing it. |
| **Procedural programming** | Organising a program as steps: data in variables, behaviour in functions. |
| **Object** | A unit that bundles data with the functions that work on it. |
| **Class** | A blueprint that describes what its objects contain and can do. |
| **Paradigm** | A style or way of organising programs, such as procedural or object-oriented. |

## Worked Examples

### Example 1: Hello, Library (strings, vectors and input)

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int main()
{
    string name;
    cout << "Your name: ";
    getline(cin, name);

    vector<string> titles = {"Python Basics", "Digital Logic", "Bangla Poems"};
    titles.push_back("World Atlas");

    cout << "Welcome, " << name << "! The library has " << titles.size() << " titles:\n";
    for (const string& t : titles) {
        cout << " - " << t << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

```input
Anika Rahman
```

```output
Your name: Welcome, Anika Rahman! The library has 4 titles:
 - Python Basics
 - Digital Logic
 - Bangla Poems
 - World Atlas
```

1. `getline(cin, name)` reads the whole line, so a name with a space works. (The prompt and the greeting run together here only because the input comes from a file; at a keyboard the Enter key you press supplies the line break.)
2. The vector starts with three titles and `push_back` adds a fourth, so `titles.size()` is 4.
3. `for (const string& t : titles)` visits each title. The `const &` avoids copying every string.
4. There is no `free` and no array size to track: the vector manages its own memory.

### Example 2: Value, reference and const reference

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

void fee_by_value(int fee) { fee += 5; }
void fee_by_reference(int& fee) { fee += 5; }

int total_letters(const vector<string>& titles)
{
    int total = 0;
    for (const string& t : titles) {
        total += static_cast<int>(t.size());
    }
    return total;
}

int main()
{
    int fee = 10;
    fee_by_value(fee);
    cout << "after fee_by_value: " << fee << '\n';
    fee_by_reference(fee);
    cout << "after fee_by_reference: " << fee << '\n';

    vector<string> titles = {"Python Basics", "Digital Logic"};
    cout << "letters in all titles: " << total_letters(titles) << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

```output
after fee_by_value: 10
after fee_by_reference: 15
letters in all titles: 26
```

1. `fee_by_value` receives a copy, so the caller's `fee` stays 10.
2. `fee_by_reference` receives the variable itself, so `fee` becomes 15.
3. `total_letters` only reads the vector, so it takes it by `const` reference: no copy, and the compiler refuses any attempt to change it.
4. "Python Basics" has 13 characters and "Digital Logic" has 13, so the total is 26.

### Example 3: Nothing protects the data

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

struct Book {
    string title;
    int copies;
};

bool borrow(Book& b)
{
    if (b.copies == 0) {
        return false;
    }
    b.copies--;
    return true;
}

int main()
{
    Book b = {"Python Basics", 1};
    cout << borrow(b) << ' ' << borrow(b) << '\n';

    b.copies = -3;   // any code is allowed to do this
    cout << b.title << " has " << b.copies << " copies\n";
    return 0;
}
```

```output
1 0
Python Basics has -3 copies
```

1. The first `borrow` succeeds (`1`) and the second fails (`0`), because no copy is left.
2. In `main`, one careless line sets `copies` to -3. The `borrow` function carefully avoided going below zero, yet nothing stops other code from doing it.
3. This is weakness 1 from the lesson. The rule "copies are never negative" lives only in the programmer's head. In Lesson 2 you will make it part of the data itself.

## Common Mistakes and Misconceptions

- **Forgetting the headers.** Using `string` without `#include <string>` or `cout` without `#include <iostream>` gives long, confusing error messages. Include what you use.
- **Mixing `cin >>` with `getline`.** After `cin >> n` the Enter key is still waiting, so the next `getline` returns an empty line. Call `cin.ignore();` first.
- **Comparing text with a pointer mindset.** With `std::string`, `a == b` compares the text. (With C character arrays it compared addresses, as you saw in Course 1.)
- **Copying a big vector by accident.** `void show(vector<string> v)` copies every string on every call. Use `const vector<string>& v`.
- **Trusting `v[i]` blindly.** `v[10]` on a vector of 3 elements is undefined behaviour, just like an array in C. Use `v.at(10)` when you want a checked access that raises an error.
- **Thinking "C++ is just C with a new name".** C++ includes C, but it is also a different way of thinking. Writing C code with `.cpp` files misses its benefits.
- **Thinking OOP throws away functions.** An object's functions, called **methods**, are still functions. OOP changes where they live and who is allowed to call them.

## Lesson Project: Library Catalogue, Procedural Version

### Objective

Build the baseline of the course project: a small **procedural** library catalogue in C++ that adds books, lists them, and lets members borrow and return copies. You will then *see* its weaknesses with your own eyes, which is the reason the next seven lessons exist.

### Requirements

- Define `struct Book` with an `id`, a `title`, an `author` and the number of `copies` on the shelf, and keep all books in one `vector<Book>`.
- Write these functions, each receiving the catalogue as a parameter (no global variables): `add_book`, `find_index` (returns -1 when the id is unknown), `print_catalogue`, `borrow_book` and `return_book`.
- Pass the catalogue by reference when a function changes it and by `const` reference when it only reads it.
- `borrow_book` and `return_book` must return `true` or `false` and print a clear message for each outcome: success, no copies left, unknown id.
- `main` runs a scripted demonstration: add three books, print the catalogue, borrow one title three times (it has two copies), borrow an unknown id, return one copy, print again, and finally set a book's copies to -5 directly.
- End the source file with a comment that lists three weaknesses of this design.

### Instructions

1. Write `struct Book` and the `add_book` function. Test it by adding one book and printing its title from `main`.
2. Write `find_index`, using a loop over the vector and returning `-1` after the loop if nothing matches.
3. Write `print_catalogue` with `<iomanip>` so that the columns line up, and call it after adding the three books.
4. Write `borrow_book` (find the book, check the copies, decrease them, print a message) and test it with every outcome.
5. Write `return_book` in the same style, then write the scripted `main` from the requirements.
6. Add the careless line `catalogue[0].copies = -5;` at the end, print the result and read it.
7. Write the three-weakness comment, and check your output against the expected output below.

### Expected Output

```text
ID    Title             Author        Copies
101   Python Basics     A. Rahman     2
102   Digital Logic     S. Karim      1
103   Bangla Poems      R. Tagore     3

Borrowed "Python Basics". Copies left: 1
Borrowed "Python Basics". Copies left: 0
"Python Basics" has no copies left.
No book with id 999.
Returned "Python Basics". Copies now: 1

ID    Title             Author        Copies
101   Python Basics     A. Rahman     1
102   Digital Logic     S. Karim      1
103   Bangla Poems      R. Tagore     3

After one careless line: Python Basics has -5 copies.
```

### Hints

1. **Hint 1 (adding a book).** `catalogue.push_back({id, title, author, copies});` builds a `Book` from the four values and appends it.
2. **Hint 2 (the loop).** Use `for (size_t i = 0; i < catalogue.size(); i++)` and convert with `static_cast<int>(i)` when you return the index.
3. **Hint 3 (aligned columns).** `cout << left << setw(6) << b.id << setw(24) << b.title;` pads each field to a fixed width.
4. **Hint 4 (the messages).** Check the unknown id first, then the missing copies, and only then change the data.
5. **Hint 5 (a compile error about `size_t`).** Add `#include <vector>` and compare an index of type `size_t` with `catalogue.size()`, not with an `int`.

### Success Criteria

- [ ] The program compiles with `-Wall -Wextra` and no warnings.
- [ ] All five functions exist, take the catalogue as a parameter, and use `&` or `const &` correctly.
- [ ] Borrowing three times from a two-copy title fails the third time with a clear message, and an unknown id is reported.
- [ ] The output matches the expected output exactly, including the final negative copy count.
- [ ] The closing comment names three real weaknesses of the design in my own words.

Add a `Member` structure with an id and a name, and a `vector<Member>`. Write `borrow_for_member` so that a member can borrow at most two books at once, which means you must also remember which books each member has. Notice how many separate vectors and functions you must now keep in step. Write down which weaknesses grew worse.

## Lesson Recap

- C++ extends C with classes, a standard library (`string`, `vector`), references and more, and you compile it with `g++`.
- Use `cin`, `cout` and `getline` for input and output; use `string` and `vector` instead of character arrays and `malloc`.
- Pass small values by value, results by reference and large read-only objects by `const` reference.
- Procedural programs keep data and functions apart, so anything can change the data, and extending them means copying code.
- Object-oriented programming bundles data with the functions allowed to change it. You will build it step by step, starting with a `Book` class in the next lesson.

Test it with a script of at least ten commands and keep the script. What would you have to change if the library also lent DVDs? Which part of your program would you most like to hide from the rest of the code, and why?

## Instructor-Guided Teaching Notes

**Pacing (60 minutes).** 10 minutes: C to C++ and `g++`. 10 minutes: iostream, strings, vectors. 10 minutes: references. 10 minutes: procedural weaknesses and the OOP idea (use Example 3 live). 20 minutes: the project, as a guided build.

**Live demonstrations.** Show the same small task in C (`printf`, `char[]`) and C++ (`cout`, `string`) side by side. Make Example 3 fail on purpose and ask the class who is "responsible" for the rule that copies are never negative.

**Misconceptions.** "References are pointers" (they are aliases and cannot be null or re-seated). "`using namespace std;` is required" (it is a convenience). "OOP is always better" (small programs are fine procedurally; the benefit grows with size).

**Assessment of the project.** Check that every function receives the catalogue as a parameter, that `const &` is used for read-only functions, that all three borrow outcomes are handled, and that the weakness comment is specific (for example "`main` can set copies to -5") rather than generic.

**Reference solution `catalogue.cpp`** (compile with `g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra catalogue.cpp -o catalogue`):

```cpp
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Book {
    int id;
    string title;
    string author;
    int copies;
};

void add_book(vector<Book>& catalogue, int id, const string& title, const string& author, int copies)
{
    catalogue.push_back({id, title, author, copies});
}

int find_index(const vector<Book>& catalogue, int id)
{
    for (size_t i = 0; i < catalogue.size(); i++) {
        if (catalogue[i].id == id) {
            return static_cast<int>(i);
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

void print_catalogue(const vector<Book>& catalogue)
{
    cout << left << setw(6) << "ID" << setw(18) << "Title" << setw(14) << "Author" << "Copies\n";
    for (const Book& b : catalogue) {
        cout << left << setw(6) << b.id << setw(18) << b.title << setw(14) << b.author << b.copies << '\n';
    }
}

bool borrow_book(vector<Book>& catalogue, int id)
{
    int i = find_index(catalogue, id);
    if (i == -1) {
        cout << "No book with id " << id << ".\n";
        return false;
    }
    if (catalogue[i].copies == 0) {
        cout << "\"" << catalogue[i].title << "\" has no copies left.\n";
        return false;
    }
    catalogue[i].copies--;
    cout << "Borrowed \"" << catalogue[i].title << "\". Copies left: " << catalogue[i].copies << '\n';
    return true;
}

bool return_book(vector<Book>& catalogue, int id)
{
    int i = find_index(catalogue, id);
    if (i == -1) {
        cout << "No book with id " << id << ".\n";
        return false;
    }
    catalogue[i].copies++;
    cout << "Returned \"" << catalogue[i].title << "\". Copies now: " << catalogue[i].copies << '\n';
    return true;
}

int main()
{
    vector<Book> catalogue;
    add_book(catalogue, 101, "Python Basics", "A. Rahman", 2);
    add_book(catalogue, 102, "Digital Logic", "S. Karim", 1);
    add_book(catalogue, 103, "Bangla Poems", "R. Tagore", 3);

    print_catalogue(catalogue);
    cout << '\n';
    borrow_book(catalogue, 101);
    borrow_book(catalogue, 101);
    borrow_book(catalogue, 101);
    borrow_book(catalogue, 999);
    return_book(catalogue, 101);
    cout << '\n';
    print_catalogue(catalogue);

    catalogue[0].copies = -5;
    cout << "\nAfter one careless line: " << catalogue[0].title << " has " << catalogue[0].copies << " copies.\n";
    return 0;
}

// Weaknesses of this design:
// 1. Any code can change any field, so "copies is never negative" is not enforced.
// 2. The data (Book) and the functions that may change it are only related by habit.
// 3. A new kind of item (a DVD) would need new functions or a long if-else chain.
```

```output
ID    Title             Author        Copies
101   Python Basics     A. Rahman     2
102   Digital Logic     S. Karim      1
103   Bangla Poems      R. Tagore     3

Borrowed "Python Basics". Copies left: 1
Borrowed "Python Basics". Copies left: 0
"Python Basics" has no copies left.
No book with id 999.
Returned "Python Basics". Copies now: 1

ID    Title             Author        Copies
101   Python Basics     A. Rahman     1
102   Digital Logic     S. Karim      1
103   Bangla Poems      R. Tagore     3

After one careless line: Python Basics has -5 copies.
```

lessons.contentMarkdown:
# Lumexa Mission Log: Object-Oriented Programming & Programming Languages

**Course/Path:** Object-Oriented Programming & Programming Languages
**Lesson:** 08 of 08
**Title:** UML Class Diagrams and Building an Object-Oriented Application
**Duration:** 60 minutes
**Difficulty:** Advanced
**Technology:** C++ (g++) · UML

---

## Mission Brief

You now have every part of a real library system: protected books, members with a lifecycle, a hierarchy of items, loans, polymorphic fees, an abstract interface, exceptions and the STL. But a pile of parts is not an application. Before a team writes code for a system this size, they **draw it**: a diagram that shows which classes exist, what each one knows and does, and how they relate. A good diagram lets a new teammate understand the whole design in five minutes, and lets the team find a design mistake *before* it costs weeks of programming.

This final lesson of the course teaches the language of those diagrams, **UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagrams**, and the process of turning requirements into a clean design. Then you assemble everything into one finished program: the **Library Management System**.

## Learning Objectives

1. Read and draw UML class diagrams: classes, attributes, methods, visibility and multiplicity.
2. Use the main UML relationships: association, aggregation, composition, inheritance, realization and dependency.
3. Turn written requirements into classes and responsibilities, using nouns, verbs and CRC cards.
4. Separate the program's logic from its user interface, and keep each class focused on one job.
5. Test an object-oriented design with assertions and review it against a checklist.
6. Assemble and document the finished Library Management System (LMS).

## Prerequisites

- Lessons 1 to 7: every object-oriented tool used in the LMS, from private data to exceptions.
- Course 1: menu-driven programs with `switch` and loops, as in the SRMS.

## Concept Explanation

### What UML is and why it helps

**UML** is a standard set of diagrams for describing software. It is a **communication tool**: a diagram is faster to read than code and lets people agree on a design before programming. UML has many kinds of diagram; in this course you will use the **class diagram** (the structure of the system) and meet the **sequence diagram** (messages between objects over time) in Course 7. Drawing a diagram is not a ritual: it is how you check your thinking.

### The class diagram: anatomy of a class

A class is drawn as a box with three compartments: its **name**, its **attributes** and its **methods**. A symbol in front of each member shows its visibility.

| Symbol | Meaning | C++ |
|---|---|---|
| `+` | public | `public:` |
| `-` | private | `private:` |
| `#` | protected | `protected:` |

Attributes are written `- name: type` and methods `+ name(parameters): returnType`. An **abstract class** has its name in *italics* (or the label «abstract»); an **interface** is labelled «interface».

```text
+-----------------------------+
| Book                        |
+-----------------------------+
| - id_: int                  |
| - title_: string            |
| - copies_: int              |
+-----------------------------+
| + borrow(): void            |
| + copies(): int             |
+-----------------------------+
```

### Relationships between classes

Lines between the boxes show how classes depend on each other. Six relationships cover almost everything:

| Relationship | Meaning | Drawn as | Library example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Association** | one class uses or knows another | plain line or arrow | a `Loan` refers to a `Member` |
| **Aggregation** | a whole has parts that can live on their own | hollow diamond at the whole | a shelf has books |
| **Composition** | a whole owns parts that die with it | filled diamond at the whole | a `Library` owns its loans |
| **Inheritance** | *is-a* (generalisation) | hollow triangle at the base | `Book` is a `LibraryItem` |
| **Realization** | a class implements an interface | dashed line, hollow triangle | `Book` implements `Borrowable` |
| **Dependency** | one class uses another briefly | dashed arrow | `Library` uses `NoCopiesError` |

The numbers at the ends of a line are **multiplicities**: `1` exactly one, `0..1` optional, `0..*` any number, `1..*` at least one. For example, one `Library` owns `0..*` loans, while each `Loan` refers to exactly `1` member and `1` item.

### From requirements to classes

A common way to find classes is to read the requirements and underline the **nouns** (candidates for classes and attributes) and the **verbs** (candidates for methods). Then test each noun: does it have its own data and behaviour that matter? A **CRC card** (Class, Responsibility, Collaborators) is an index card for one class: its name, what it is responsible for, and the other classes it works with. If a card needs more than a handful of responsibilities, the class is probably doing too much. This is the **single responsibility principle**: a class should have one clear reason to change.

### Building the application in layers

Keep three layers apart:

1. **Model**: the classes of the domain (`LibraryItem`, `Member`, `Loan`) and their rules.
2. **Manager**: one class (here `Library`) that holds the collections and coordinates the model, offering operations such as `borrow(member, item)`.
3. **Interface**: the menu, the keyboard and the screen (`main`). It calls the manager and prints results.

Keeping the interface separate means the same `Library` could be driven by a menu, a web page or an automatic test, without change. Real projects also split each class into a header (`.h`) and a source (`.cpp`) file and compile them together (`g++ a.cpp b.cpp -o app`); the single-file layout in this lesson is only for convenience.

### Testing and reviewing an object-oriented design

A class that can be tested alone is a well-designed class. Write small tests that create objects, call methods and check results with `assert` (from `<cassert>`), including the failure cases. Then review the design with a checklist: Is every attribute private? Does each constructor leave a valid object? Is shared code written once (inheritance)? Does polymorphism replace type tests? Are failures reported with exceptions? Does each class have one job? Are the names clear?

## Key Vocabulary

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **UML** | The Unified Modeling Language: a standard notation for diagrams of software. |
| **Class diagram** | A UML diagram of classes, their members and the relationships between them. |
| **Visibility** | The `+`, `-` or `#` symbol that shows whether a member is public, private or protected. |
| **Association** | A relationship in which one class uses or refers to another. |
| **Aggregation / composition** | Whole-part relationships; composition means the parts die with the whole. |
| **Multiplicity** | The number of objects that can take part in a relationship, such as `0..*`. |
| **CRC card** | A card listing a class's name, responsibilities and collaborators. |
| **Single responsibility** | The principle that a class should have one clear reason to change. |
| **Facade / manager class** | A class that coordinates other classes and offers simple operations to the outside. |
| **Unit test** | A small program that checks one class or function against known results. |

## Worked Examples

### Example 1: From requirements to classes

Here are the library's requirements, written in plain English:

> The library lends **books**, **magazines** and **DVDs**. Each item has an id and a title, and a number of copies. A **member** may borrow up to three items at a time. When a member borrows an item, the library records a **loan** with a due date. When the item is returned late, the member pays a **late fee** that depends on the kind of item.

1. **Underline the nouns:** library, book, magazine, DVD, item, id, title, copies, member, loan, due date, late fee, kind of item.
2. **Sort them.** *Classes*: Library, Book, Magazine, DVD, Item, Member, Loan. *Attributes*: id, title, copies, due date. *Not classes*: late fee (a calculated value, a method of the item), kind (a method that tells you the class).
3. **Underline the verbs:** lends, borrow, record, return, pay. They become the methods `borrow()`, `give_back()`, `late_fee()` and the manager's `borrow(member, item)`.
4. **Find the relationships:** Book, Magazine and DVD *are* items (inheritance); a Loan *refers to* one member and one item (association); the Library *owns* its items, members and loans (composition).
5. **Write a CRC card** for the `Library`: responsibility "lend and take back items, enforce the limit of three loans"; collaborators "LibraryItem, Member, Loan".

The result is the design you will draw in the project, and it matches the classes you built in Lessons 2 to 6.

### Example 2: From UML to C++

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

struct Loan {
    int member_id;
    int item_id;
};

class Library {
private:
    vector<Loan> loans_;

public:
    void add_loan(int member_id, int item_id) { loans_.push_back({member_id, item_id}); }

    int loans_of(int member_id) const
    {
        int count = 0;
        for (const Loan& l : loans_) {
            if (l.member_id == member_id) {
                count++;
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    int total() const { return static_cast<int>(loans_.size()); }
};

int main()
{
    Library lib;
    lib.add_loan(1, 101);
    lib.add_loan(1, 301);
    lib.add_loan(2, 301);
    cout << "total loans: " << lib.total() << '\n';
    cout << "member 1 holds " << lib.loans_of(1) << ", member 2 holds " << lib.loans_of(2) << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

```output
total loans: 3
member 1 holds 2, member 2 holds 1
```

1. The diagram says "a `Library` owns `0..*` loans" (composition). In code that becomes a private `vector<Loan>` inside `Library`, with no way for outside code to reach it directly.
2. "A `Loan` refers to one member and one item" (association) becomes two plain ids. The loan does not own the member or the item.
3. The multiplicity `0..*` tells you to use a container, not a single variable.
4. `loans_of` answers a question about the whole collection, which only the `Library` can do. Putting such operations in the manager class is exactly its job.

### Example 3: Testing a class with assertions

```cpp
#include <cassert>
#include <iostream>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
using namespace std;

class Book {
private:
    string title_;
    int copies_;

public:
    Book(const string& title, int copies) : title_(title), copies_(copies)
    {
        if (title.empty()) {
            throw invalid_argument("title must not be empty");
        }
        if (copies < 0) {
            throw invalid_argument("copies must not be negative");
        }
    }
    int copies() const { return copies_; }
    bool borrow()
    {
        if (copies_ == 0) {
            return false;
        }
        copies_--;
        return true;
    }
};

int main()
{
    Book b("Python Basics", 1);
    assert(b.copies() == 1);
    assert(b.borrow() == true);
    assert(b.copies() == 0);
    assert(b.borrow() == false);
    assert(b.copies() == 0);

    bool threw = false;
    try {
        Book bad("", 3);
    } catch (const invalid_argument&) {
        threw = true;
    }
    assert(threw);

    cout << "all tests passed\n";
    return 0;
}
```

```output
all tests passed
```

1. Each `assert` states something that must be true. If one is false, the program stops at once and names the failing line.
2. The tests cover the normal case (borrowing succeeds), the boundary (the last copy) and the failure cases (no copies left, invalid data).
3. Because `Book` has no menu and no printing of its own, it can be tested without a keyboard. That is what the layered design buys you.
4. Run the tests again after every change: they tell you at once if a change broke an old rule (a regression).

## Common Mistakes and Misconceptions

- **Drawing the code instead of the design.** A class diagram with every helper function and every `int i` is unreadable. Show the important attributes, the public methods and the relationships.
- **Confusing inheritance with association.** An arrow with a hollow triangle means *is-a*. A plain arrow means *uses* or *knows*. A `Loan` is not a kind of `Member`.
- **Using every relationship everywhere.** Aggregation versus composition is a fine distinction. If unsure, use a plain association and say what you mean in a label.
- **Forgetting multiplicities.** "A member has loans" says nothing; "0..3" tells the programmer about a rule.
- **One giant "God" class.** A class that knows everything is hard to change and test. Give each class one job.
- **Mixing the menu with the logic.** A `Library` that calls `cin` and `cout` everywhere cannot be tested or reused. Keep input and output in `main`.
- **Designing and never revising.** A diagram is a draft. When the code shows the design is wrong, change the diagram too.
- **Skipping the tests for failures.** Test what must *fail* (empty title, no copies) as carefully as what must work.

## Guided Hands-On Activity

**Design it before you build it.** Work with your teacher.

1. On paper, draw the class box for `LibraryItem`: its attributes and methods with `+` and `-`, and mark it abstract. Then draw `Book`, `Magazine` and `DVD` below it with inheritance arrows.
2. Add `Member`, `Loan` and `Library`. Connect them with the relationships from the table, and write a multiplicity at every end.
3. Type Example 2. Add a method `bool has_loan(int member_id, int item_id) const` to `Library` and test it. Does the UML diagram need to change?
4. Type Example 3 and make a test fail on purpose: change one `assert` so it is wrong, run it, and read the message. Then restore it.
5. Add two more tests to Example 3: one that a book with 2 copies can be borrowed twice, and one that a negative number of copies is rejected.
6. Write a CRC card for `Member`. Does it have more than three responsibilities? If so, which should move to another class?

## Lesson Project: LMS Capstone

### Objective

Finish the course project: draw the **UML class diagram** of the Library Management System, and assemble all the classes from Lessons 2 to 6 into one complete, menu-driven C++ application that uses inheritance, polymorphism, exceptions, templates and the STL, with a clean separation of logic and interface.

### Requirements

- A UML class diagram (on paper or in a drawing tool) with at least these classes: `LibraryItem` (abstract), `Book`, `Magazine`, `DVD`, `Member`, `Loan` and `Library`, with visibility symbols, multiplicities and the right relationship for each pair.
- `LibraryItem` is abstract, with a virtual destructor and the pure virtual methods `kind()` and `late_fee(int days)`. The late fees are 5, 2 and 10 per day for books, magazines and DVDs.
- A hierarchy of exceptions derived from `LibraryError`: not found, no copies left and loan limit reached (3).
- `Library` owns the items (`unique_ptr`), the members and the loans. It offers `borrow`, `give_back`, `list_items` and `report`, and throws exceptions for every failure. It never reads input.
- A function template that looks up an id in any `map` and throws `NotFoundError` if it is missing.
- `main` is the menu: `1` list items, `2` borrow, `3` return (with the day of return, so a late fee can be charged), `4` loans report, `0` exit. It catches `LibraryError` and prints the message.
- Every loan lasts 14 days from day 1.

### Instructions

1. Draw the class diagram first, then compare it with the classes you plan to write.
2. Write the exception classes and `LibraryItem` with its three derived classes.
3. Write the lookup template and the `Library` class with `borrow`, one operation at a time, testing each with a few lines in `main`.
4. Add `give_back` (find the loan with `find_if`, calculate the days late, charge the fee through the item's `late_fee`) and the reports.
5. Write the menu in `main`: a loop with a `switch`, a `try`/`catch` around each command, and a message for an invalid choice.
6. Run the program with the scripted input below, and compare your output with the expected output.
7. Write a README comment at the top of the file: what the system does, how to compile it, the commands, and the three classes you are proudest of.

### Expected Output

### Hints

1. **Hint 1 (the lookup template).** `template <typename Map> auto& find_or_throw(Map& m, int id, const string& what) { auto it = m.find(id); if (it == m.end()) throw NotFoundError(what, id); return it->second; }`.
2. **Hint 2 (the limit).** Count the member's loans with `count_if` before you call `item.take()`, so a refused loan changes nothing.
3. **Hint 3 (the late fee).** `int late = max(0, today - loan.due_day); int fee = item.late_fee(late);`.
4. **Hint 4 (removing a loan).** `loans_.erase(it);` where `it` came from `find_if`.
5. **Hint 5 (reading the menu).** Read the command with `cin >> choice` and the numbers of that command with `cin >> member >> item`.

### Success Criteria

- [ ] The UML diagram shows every class with visibility, multiplicities and the correct relationships, and matches the code.
- [ ] The program uses inheritance, polymorphism, exceptions, a template and STL algorithms, and the `Library` class contains no input or output of its own other than the messages it is asked to print.
- [ ] Every failure (not found, no copies, limit reached, no such loan) is an exception that is caught and reported, and a refused action changes nothing.
- [ ] The late fee of the returned DVD is 50 (5 days late at 10 per day).
- [ ] The code compiles with `-Wall -Wextra` with no warnings, and the output matches the expected output.

### Extension Challenge

Add a `save` command that writes the loans to a text file and a `load` command that reads them back (reusing the idea from the SRMS in Course 1). ## Lesson Recap

- **UML class diagrams** show classes (name, attributes, methods), visibility (`+`, `-`, `#`) and relationships with multiplicities.
- The six relationships are association, aggregation, composition, inheritance, realization and dependency; inheritance is only for *is-a*.
- Find classes from the **nouns**, methods from the **verbs**, and check each class against the **single responsibility** idea (CRC cards help).
- Keep three layers apart: **model**, **manager** and **interface**, so the logic can be tested and reused.
- Test classes with assertions, including the failure cases, and review the design against a checklist. You have now built a complete object-oriented application.

## Homework / Extension Mission

Finish the capstone and prepare a five-minute presentation of the LMS: the UML diagram on one slide or page, a live run of the scripted session, and two design decisions you are proud of (for example "late fees live in the items, so a new kind of item needs no change to `Library`"). Write one page of reflection: what was the hardest bug, which rule from Lessons 2 to 6 saved you the most trouble, and how does this design compare with your procedural catalogue from Lesson 1? Compare it with the three weaknesses you wrote then, and tick off each one that is now solved.

## Course Project Connection

This lesson **is** the course project: the finished **Library Management System using C++**. Lesson 1's procedural catalogue became protected `Book` objects (Lesson 2), members with a lifecycle (Lesson 3), an inheritance hierarchy with loans (Lesson 4), polymorphic fees (Lesson 5), a safe core with an interface, a template, exceptions and STL containers (Lesson 6), and a Java port (Lesson 7). Today they are one application with a diagram. Keep the diagram and the code in your portfolio: in Course 3 you will analyse the efficiency of the data structures behind such a system, and in Course 7 you will give it a database and a web interface.

## Instructor-Guided Teaching Notes

**Pacing (60 minutes).** 10 minutes: UML notation, with the `Book` box on the board. 10 minutes: relationships and multiplicities (draw the library diagram together, then the table). 10 minutes: requirements to classes (Example 1). 30 minutes: the project; most of the build continues at home, with the diagram drawn first.

**Live demonstrations.** Draw one wrong diagram on purpose (an inheritance arrow from `Loan` to `Member`) and ask the class to find the problem. Run the tests of Example 3 and break one rule live. Compile the final program with `-fsanitize=address,undefined` to show that it is clean.

**Misconceptions.** "UML is only for big companies." "A diagram must be perfect before coding." "Composition and aggregation are interchangeable." "The `Library` class should print its own messages."

**Assessment of the project.** Mark the diagram and the code together: do they agree? Check the layering, the exceptions, the template and the tests, and ask each student to explain one design decision. The diagram should show multiplicities such as `Library 1 — 0..* Loan`.

**Reference solution `lms.cpp`** (compile with `g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra lms.cpp -o lms`; the input below is typed into the menu):

```cpp
// Library Management System: a menu-driven application in C++.
// Compile: g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra lms.cpp -o lms
// Commands: 1 list items | 2 borrow (member item) | 3 return (member item day) | 4 loans | 0 exit
#include <algorithm>
#include <cassert>
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <memory>
#include <stdexcept>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

class LibraryError : public runtime_error {
public:
    using runtime_error::runtime_error;
};

class NotFoundError : public LibraryError {
public:
    NotFoundError(const string& what, int id) : LibraryError(what + " " + to_string(id) + " not found") {}
};

class NoCopiesError : public LibraryError {
public:
    explicit NoCopiesError(const string& title) : LibraryError("no copies left of \"" + title + "\"") {}
};

class LimitError : public LibraryError {
public:
    explicit LimitError(const string& name) : LibraryError(name + " has reached the limit of 3 loans") {}
};

class LibraryItem {
private:
    int id_;
    string title_;
    int copies_;

public:
    LibraryItem(int id, const string& title, int copies) : id_(id), title_(title), copies_(copies) {}
    virtual ~LibraryItem() = default;

    int id() const { return id_; }
    const string& title() const { return title_; }
    int copies() const { return copies_; }

    void take()
    {
        if (copies_ == 0) {
            throw NoCopiesError(title_);
        }
        copies_--;
    }
    void put_back() { copies_++; }

    virtual string kind() const = 0;
    virtual int late_fee(int days) const = 0;

    string describe() const
    {
        return kind() + " #" + to_string(id_) + " \"" + title_ + "\" (copies: " + to_string(copies_) + ")";
    }
};

class Book : public LibraryItem {
public:
    using LibraryItem::LibraryItem;
    string kind() const override { return "Book"; }
    int late_fee(int days) const override { return 5 * days; }
};

class Magazine : public LibraryItem {
public:
    using LibraryItem::LibraryItem;
    string kind() const override { return "Magazine"; }
    int late_fee(int days) const override { return 2 * days; }
};

class DVD : public LibraryItem {
public:
    using LibraryItem::LibraryItem;
    string kind() const override { return "DVD"; }
    int late_fee(int days) const override { return 10 * days; }
};

class Member {
private:
    int id_;
    string name_;

public:
    Member(int id, const string& name) : id_(id), name_(name) {}
    int id() const { return id_; }
    const string& name() const { return name_; }
};

struct Loan {
    int member_id;
    int item_id;
    int due_day;
};

template <typename Map>
auto& find_or_throw(Map& m, int id, const string& what)
{
    auto it = m.find(id);
    if (it == m.end()) {
        throw NotFoundError(what, id);
    }
    return it->second;
}

class Library {
private:
    static constexpr int LOAN_DAYS = 14;
    static constexpr int MAX_LOANS = 3;

    map<int, unique_ptr<LibraryItem>> items_;
    map<int, Member> members_;
    vector<Loan> loans_;

public:
    void add_item(unique_ptr<LibraryItem> item)
    {
        int id = item->id();
        items_[id] = move(item);
    }
    void add_member(int id, const string& name) { members_.emplace(id, Member(id, name)); }

    void list_items() const
    {
        for (const auto& entry : items_) {
            cout << "  " << entry.second->describe() << '\n';
        }
    }

    void borrow(int member_id, int item_id, int today)
    {
        const string& name = find_or_throw(members_, member_id, "member").name();
        LibraryItem& item = *find_or_throw(items_, item_id, "item");
        int count = static_cast<int>(count_if(loans_.begin(), loans_.end(), [&](const Loan& l) { return l.member_id == member_id; }));
        if (count >= MAX_LOANS) {
            throw LimitError(name);
        }
        item.take();
        loans_.push_back({member_id, item_id, today + LOAN_DAYS});
        cout << name << " borrowed " << item.kind() << " \"" << item.title() << "\", due day " << today + LOAN_DAYS << '\n';
    }

    void give_back(int member_id, int item_id, int today)
    {
        const string& name = find_or_throw(members_, member_id, "member").name();
        LibraryItem& item = *find_or_throw(items_, item_id, "item");
        auto it = find_if(loans_.begin(), loans_.end(), [&](const Loan& l) { return l.member_id == member_id && l.item_id == item_id; });
        if (it == loans_.end()) {
            throw NotFoundError("loan of item", item_id);
        }
        int late = max(0, today - it->due_day);
        int fee = item.late_fee(late);
        loans_.erase(it);
        item.put_back();
        cout << name << " returned \"" << item.title() << "\" on day " << today << ". Late days: " << late << ", fee: " << fee << '\n';
    }

    void report() const
    {
        if (loans_.empty()) {
            cout << "  no loans\n";
            return;
        }
        vector<Loan> sorted = loans_;
        sort(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), [](const Loan& a, const Loan& b) { return a.due_day < b.due_day; });
        for (const Loan& l : sorted) {
            cout << "  " << members_.at(l.member_id).name() << " has \"" << items_.at(l.item_id)->title() << "\", due day " << l.due_day << '\n';
        }
    }
};

void run_tests()
{
    Library lib;
    lib.add_member(1, "Test");
    lib.add_item(make_unique<Book>(1, "Test Book", 1));
    bool threw = false;
    try {
        lib.borrow(9, 1, 1);
    } catch (const NotFoundError&) {
        threw = true;
    }
    assert(threw);
    assert(Book(1, "x", 1).late_fee(3) == 15);
    assert(Magazine(2, "y", 1).late_fee(3) == 6);
    assert(DVD(3, "z", 1).late_fee(3) == 30);
    assert(DVD(3, "z", 1).kind() == "DVD");
}

int main()
{
    run_tests();

    Library lib;
    lib.add_item(make_unique<Book>(101, "Python Basics", 2));
    lib.add_item(make_unique<Magazine>(201, "Science Today", 1));
    lib.add_item(make_unique<DVD>(301, "How Computers Work", 1));
    lib.add_member(1, "Anika");
    lib.add_member(2, "Rafi");

    int choice = -1;
    while (true) {
        cout << "\nLMS menu: 1 Items | 2 Borrow | 3 Return | 4 Loans | 0 Exit\nChoice:\n";
        if (!(cin >> choice) || choice == 0) {
            break;
        }
        try {
            switch (choice) {
            case 1:
                lib.list_items();
                break;
            case 2: {
                int member = 0;
                int item = 0;
                cin >> member >> item;
                lib.borrow(member, item, 1);
                break;
            }
            case 3: {
                int member = 0;
                int item = 0;
                int day = 0;
                cin >> member >> item >> day;
                lib.give_back(member, item, day);
                break;
            }
            case 4:
                lib.report();
                break;
            default:
                cout << "Please choose a number from 0 to 4.\n";
            }
        } catch (const LibraryError& e) {
            cout << "Error: " << e.what() << '\n';
        }
    }
    cout << "Goodbye!\n";
    return 0;
}
```
